content:
Allison Grant: We keep getting stuck on this during incidents: do we ever mark a component “Degraded performance” on latency-only (no 5xx spike)? Or do we require errors to avoid flapping/false positives?

Aisha Bello: +1. Our current public components are mostly error-driven bc it’s unambiguous. But tail latency can be brutal and still show 200s.

Caleb Johnson: The issue is “latency-only” is usually not actually latency-only. If clients have timeouts, we’ll see 499/408/504 depending on where. But yeah, in practice it’s messy.

Christine Wong: From comms POV, customers don’t care whether it’s 5xx vs p99=40s. If they’re timing out, they call it down. Status page saying “Operational” looks bad.

Logan Wright: Mechanically: our status automation hooks are wired to error% and burn alerts right now. Latency thresholds are noisier across routes/models, and regions have different baselines.

Rafael Mendes: I’m fine with latency criteria, but it needs to be very explicit + anti-flap. Otherwise on-call gets paged to “update statuspage” for a 6 min p95 wobble.

Mina Haddad: Also important: do we want to expose latency degradation when only one region is impacted (e.g. us-east)? I assume yes, but then we need per-region component rules consistent.

Allison Grant: Yep per-region components are the plan. Question is the “is this degraded?” rubric.

Aisha Bello: Proposal: allow latency-based degradation only when it’s sustained and SLO-relevant. i.e. if latency SLO burn rate triggers for the component, it can drive status.

Caleb Johnson: Burn rate alerts are better than raw thresholds. But note: not all components have a latency SLO defined yet (esp streaming).

Devon Price: For incident-bot, easiest is: status update suggestion is triggered if ANY of (error threshold, burn-rate alert, operator manual override). Latency-only could come in via burn-rate.

Logan Wright: A pure latency rule might still be needed for cases where customers see slow but we’re under error budget because requests eventually succeed.

Rafael Mendes: That’s the crux: do we want “degraded” to mean “SLO is at risk” or “customer experience is materially worse”? Those diverge.

Christine Wong: For public comms, “materially worse experience” is what customers read. We can word it carefully without promising SLA.

Allison Grant: Ok, let’s define criteria for “Degraded performance” (public) that can be driven by either errors OR latency/timeout symptoms.

Aisha Bello: Concrete suggestion:
- Error-based: if 5xx (or non-2xx excluding 429) > 1% for 10m at component+region.
- Latency-based: if p95 latency > 2x trailing 7d baseline for 15m AND volume > N req/min.
But I’d like a tie-breaker to avoid “baseline drift” and random model mix shifts.

Caleb Johnson: Baseline ratio helps, but on big launches baseline itself shifts. Also p95 is not enough; customers feel p99. But p99 is too spiky.

Logan Wright: What about using “% requests over timeout threshold” instead of latency percentiles? Like % > 30s for chat, % > 60s for long gen, etc.

Mina Haddad: Timeout threshold differs by capability though (streaming vs non-streaming). Streaming “latency” is more like time-to-first-token (TTFT) + disconnect rate.

Allison Grant: Right. So maybe:
- Chat/Generate (non-streaming): latency rule uses p95 + “over 30s” bucket.
- Streaming: use TTFT p95 + disconnect rate.
- Embeddings/rerank: p95 latency + error.

Rafael Mendes: I want something that’s implementable this quarter. We can’t ship 12 bespoke rules and then everyone bikesheds thresholds.

Aisha Bello: Keep it simple: a single latency-only gate for now:
“Degraded performance may be declared if latency SLO burn-rate (2h window) > 2x AND sustained for 10m, even if error% < threshold.”
That way we piggyback on SLO definitions and anti-flap.

Caleb Johnson: +1, but note: if a component doesn’t have latency SLO, it won’t trigger. But that’s okay; we can fill gaps as we mature.

Christine Wong: Works for comms: we can say “We’re observing elevated latency/timeouts for <component> in <region>” without implying outage.

Logan Wright: We should add one more explicit “timeouts/retries” signal because customers do time out while our upstream sees 200. Example: mobile clients drop the connection.

Allison Grant: Can we treat that as “error-based” via 499/timeout buckets? If yes, it’s not “latency-only” anyway.

Caleb Johnson: Yep. If we count gateway 499/504 as “customer-impact errors” (separate from app 5xx), then the ambiguity reduces.

Rafael Mendes: OK, decision proposal:
1) Public “Degraded Performance” can be driven by either:
   a) error-based thresholds (5xx or elevated 499/504/timeouts) OR
   b) latency SLO burn-rate alerts (component+region) with anti-flap.
2) We do NOT mark degraded on raw latency percentiles alone unless it maps to an SLO/burn.
3) Streaming uses TTFT SLO where defined; otherwise rely on disconnect/timeouts.

Mina Haddad: +1, and we should document “latency-only” as “latency SLO burn” so it’s not subjective.

Aisha Bello: +1. I’ll update the signal standard doc to explicitly allow latency burn-rate → status degraded, and specify the anti-flap (10m sustained + 15m clear).

Christine Wong: Please add a short phrasing guide too. Something like:
“Elevated latency and increased timeouts affecting <capability> in <region>. Requests may take longer than usual.”
Avoid “SLA breach” language.

Devon Price: For incident-bot: I can add an optional field “customer_timeouts_observed=yes/no” that influences the suggested template. But the trigger stays burn/error-based.

Allison Grant: Sounds good. Action items:
- Aisha: draft criteria + thresholds wording (esp 499/504 inclusion) and send for review.
- Caleb/Logan: confirm which metrics we can reliably tag per component+region for timeouts.
- Devon: note this in incident-bot logic (no raw p95 trigger).

Rafael Mendes: +1. Let’s keep it tight and avoid new on-call burden. If the rule can’t be automated and audited, it shouldn’t be a “must-update statuspage” trigger.

Allison Grant: Agreed. I’ll post summary in #eng-sre too so folks stop debating this mid-incident.
